claims.statement: Sesam documents two separate security domains: user roles and permissions authorize people to perform actions, while secrets hold integration credentials such as database passwords.
Portal roles are assigned to users within individual subscriptions, while node permissions are assigned to roles on pipes, systems, and datasets and evaluated against the user's roles.

In the documented GUI login flow, the portal checks the user's email and password, returns subscriptions where the user has a role, and issues a JWT containing the roles for the selected subscription signed with the portal's private key.

The node validates the JWT signature using the portal's public key and checks the requested dataset's ACL for Read data permission; a permitted read returns contents and an ACL denial returns 403 Forbidden.

Most service API calls require a JWT sent on each request in the Authorization header as Bearer followed by the token, and clients must use the actual subscription connection URL, typically a hosted URL ending in /api.

The portal provides GET /api/jwt for the logged-in user, POST /api/jwt with email/password and optional subscription_id, a subscription-specific JWT GET endpoint, and an RSA public-key endpoint; omitting subscription_id from POST requests a JWT for all the user's subscriptions.

The published role overview grants Admin all listed management capabilities and Developer subscription/resource/role/permission management and config uploads, but excludes Developer from admin, other-user, ACL, and license management.
The role overview allows User to manage own pipes and systems and manage datasets, while Guest can only view pipes and systems and has no dataset management capability.

Pipe and system configuration permissions are lists of three-element ACL entries containing an allow/deny action, a group or role list, and a permission list; prose uses ALLOW/DENY while published JSON examples use lowercase allow/deny.

The documented pipe Developer ACL grant distinguishes read_config, write_config, run_pump_operation, read_data, and write_data, while the system grant distinguishes read_data, write_data, read_config, write_config, read_proxy, and write_proxy.
A newly created pipe inherits the creator's roles and stores those roles in its configuration.
Runtime permission checks verify that a pipe may read its source system and write its target system; a failed check fails the pipe run and displays an error on the pipe's GUI page.

The portal supports listing, creating, and updating subscription API JWTs intended for scripts and cron jobs; creation requires exp and principals, and a token-specific DELETE endpoint removes an API JWT.

An API JWT's configured exp is an epoch expiration date without refresh_interval; with refresh_interval it is the last refreshable time, while the signed token expires at current_time plus refresh_interval.

Subscription API JWT jwt_string is returned only on creation; refresh-enabled tokens have client_id and client_secret, with client_secret also returned only on creation, so later token listings do not recover those credentials.

The portal's POST /api/openid_connect/token accepts form data with client_credentials or refresh_token grant_type and client_id/client_secret; this portal authentication surface is distinct from a remote provider token_url configured on an outbound URL system.

The subscription revoked_json_web_tokens feed is intended for nodes to learn about changed user permissions and revoked API JWTs, covers transient GUI and long-lived API JWTs, and supports continuation using the last entity's _updated value as since.
JWT revocation records identify either user_principal or api_token_id, never both, and api_token_id identifies one specific API JWT to invalidate.

Every pipe and system is assigned a config group using metadata.$config-group for individual endpoints or the URL for grouped bulk endpoints; omission selects the default group, which is also used by /api/config.

PUT /api/config and PUT /api/config/{config-group} replace all configuration in the selected group, while PUT /api/config-all replaces all groups; config groups define configuration replacement scope rather than the role principals used by resource ACLs.

The default-group and all-group configuration PUT APIs document force=true as accepting configuration errors and applying configuration on a best-effort basis, with default false and a warning that this is rarely a good idea.
Secrets are write-only credentials: uploaded original values cannot be extracted, only secret names can be listed, and operators must securely retain original values off-site for later re-upload.
The secrets manager stores secret values internally in encrypted form using a key unique to each Sesam instance.
System-local secrets are visible to one specified system and are recommended; global secrets are available to all systems but are not recommended.
Global secrets live until explicitly deleted, while system-local secrets also disappear when their system is removed; deleting and re-adding a system requires uploading its local secrets again.
Secret-upload API payloads are JSON objects mapping names to string values, although the narrative security guide also mentions lists of objects.
Global and system secret GET APIs return names rather than values, and DELETE /secrets/{secret_key} or /systems/{system_id}/secrets/{secret_key} removes the named secret in the corresponding scope.
The global secret PUT contract adds submitted secrets and overwrites matching names; global POST explicitly adds or overwrites submitted secrets without deleting existing secrets.

System-local secret PUT overwrites the secrets for that system, whereas POST adds or overwrites named values without deleting existing secrets, making POST the explicitly additive operation for a targeted rotation.
The documented CLI put-secrets and get-secrets commands address system-local scope when given a system ID and global scope without it; get-secrets outputs key names only.
Secret references use $SECRET(key) in supported System configuration locations only, with substituted values used as needed at runtime rather than exposed through the configuration API.
Environment variables use $ENV(variable) for nonsensitive configuration parameters, are global only, and apply to System, Pipe, and service metadata configuration entities.
Multiple secret or environment references can be composed into a property and mixed with each other, but cannot be nested; properties composed from multiple references are always strings.
URL systems provide HTTP/HTTPS session handling, connection pooling, and authentication for sources and sinks, and REST systems extend URL systems and inherit all URL configuration properties.

Outbound URL-system authentication is opt-in with none by default; documented modes are basic, digest, ntlm, tripletex, and jwt, and a username requires both a selected authentication protocol and a password to have effect.
Outbound jwt authentication requires jwt_token for the remote server, and using jwt_token overwrites a supplied Authorization header.
REST system default header keys can be overridden by operation-level headers but cannot be discarded.

URL-system oauth2 supports client-credentials and refresh-token grants, requires client_id/client_secret/token_url, additionally requires access_token/refresh_token for refresh-token grants, and supports scope, extra token-request parameters, and a refresh_window defaulting to 30 seconds.
URL-system oauth2 cannot be combined with JWT authentication or jwt_token, and its contract requires TLS-secured transport for both the token endpoint and the target url_pattern.
Tripletex outbound authentication requires consumer_token, employee_token, and token_url, defaults ttl to 48 hours, and automatically attempts to refresh expired access tokens.

URL-system proxy configuration supports HTTP(S) and SOCKS5 proxies with optional embedded authentication, and the contract instructs operators to keep embedded proxy username/password values in system secrets.

Experimental REST custom_auth uses a required get_token_operation and optional earlier get_refresh_token_operation; responses from both are available through Jinja's token object, while initial_refresh_token values are immediately available and later overwritten by fetched refresh tokens.

REST custom_auth requires an absolute-date expires_at_expression or a seconds-valued expires_in_expression, gives valid absolute expiry precedence, defaults refresh_window to 30 seconds, and requires corresponding refresh-token expiry configuration when a refresh-token operation is used.

REST custom-auth token response properties can construct business-operation payloads, headers, and parameters through the token object; access_token_property and refresh_token_property helpers are deprecated in favor of direct token references.

For on-premise single subscriptions, newly fetched custom-auth refresh tokens are kept only in memory; after reboot pipes fail if a new refresh token had been fetched, and initial_refresh_token must be manually updated to that new token.

URL-system verify_ssl and service metadata global_defaults.verify_ssl are documented with default false; custom_ca_pem_chain supplies verification certificates only when verify_ssl is true, and REST inherits these TLS settings.

The hosted architecture places an Azure Network Security Group in front of cloud services with only service-API port 443 openable, and a reverse proxy terminates TLS and routes traffic using Let's Encrypt-managed certificates; the single-machine description also allows user-provided certificates.

The network-policy feature supports blocking all public access or allowing only listed IP addresses/ranges; the described new architecture supports reverse-proxy IP allowlisting and custom pipe rules for public and restricted access.
The network-policy reference explicitly states that outgoing traffic currently has no restrictions, so that feature is not a documented egress allowlist.

Portal network settings expose public-access and network-acl; a network ACL entry requires address and optionally supplies access as Allow or Deny and description, using an object format distinct from resource permission ACL tuples.
The hosted isolation reference describes subscriptions on separate isolated hardware but subscriptions within the same subscription group sharing a network.

VPN uses IPSec to extend Sesam into an on-premises network, is enabled under Subscription Products in Management Studio, and requires configuring the peer gateway/address spaces plus the on-premises gateway address, routed address spaces, and a pre-shared authentication key; VPN has an additional surcharge.

Developer subscriptions do not support VPN, while multi and flexi subscriptions support advanced highly available VPN setups with redundant BGP-enabled connections and custom IPSec rules arranged through support.
The dedicated BYOK reference documents hosted disks and remote geo-replicated backup storage as encrypted by platform-managed keys by default.

The BYOK feature has Sesam manage a revocable encryption key, generally requires data to be reloadable after revocation, and is opt-in through support for new single subscriptions but not supported for multi subscriptions.

The general hosted-architecture page says BYOK is not supported, while the dedicated BYOK feature documents scoped single-subscription support; this discrepancy prevents treating either as a universal deployment guarantee.

The hosted monitoring reference describes shipping service errors, health/status, kernel logs, and configuration without embedded data or secrets, and shipping the pipe execution dataset only with pipe monitoring enabled; entity objects attached to failing execution logs are not shipped to Sesam.
The hosted metrics path pushes Prometheus-compatible resource telemetry from local virtual machines to Sesam for monitoring and operations.
REST and HTTP-endpoint tracing default to off and can record request/response headers and body prefixes in pipe execution events when enabled.

Despite the security guide's ordinary secret-substitution nonexposure promise, REST and metadata trace redaction is explicitly best effort with possible leakage; log_secret_redacted_bytes defaults to 600 and -1 requests full redaction, while HTTP endpoint tracing describes that setting specifically for the Authorization request header.
Subscription termination deletes subscription data and backups except for the documented single-machine Azure backup retention of 30 days after deletion.
For self-hosted services, the owner is responsible for off-site backups of checkpoint directories or the virtual machine.

The CI guide requires a designated CI node and serialized tests because testing overwrites configuration; the CI node must be unable to write externally and at minimum must lack the variables and secrets needed for output-system connections.

The Sesam client is intended for personal testing and CI/CD subscriptions, permits only one client command instance per subscription, warns against manual changes while it runs, and explicitly warns not to run it on production subscriptions.
Local configuration testing guidance requires output pipes to be disabled or unable to send to their external systems while the other pipes are run to completion.
